lessons.title: Why we study Economics: the seven reasons the scheme states and the two-paragraph answer
objectives: State what the opening line of the topic says Economics studies and name the three agents it gives
Give the seven reasons the source states for studying Economics, each with the line that states it
Write the two-paragraph answer the Week 1 EVALUATION asks for, using only the reasons the source states
lessons.body:
WHY WE STUDY ECONOMICS

What you will learn: what the school's own note says Economics studies, the seven reasons it gives for studying the subject, and how to write the two-paragraph answer the same note sets as an EVALUATION question.

This lesson stays inside Week 1 of the scheme. Each of the seven reasons carries the line of the source that states it, so a reader can find it. The reasons are explained here in new words; the note itself is not reproduced, and no example, figure, occupation or career promise has been added, because the source gives none for this topic.

1. WHAT THE SUBJECT IS HERE FOR
Before its list, the note opens the topic with one lead line. That line (line 84) puts Economics among the social sciences and says that it studies the way people behave in the ordinary business of life, naming three kinds of agent: the individual, the firm and the government. The rest of the lead line then hands the topic over to a set of reasons, and those reasons - seven separate lines, printed without numbers - are the teaching point of this lesson.

2. THE SEVEN REASONS, EACH WITH ITS LINE
Reason one - the student is given the basic skill of analysing an economic problem, and the source ties that skill to being better prepared for any post in which economic decisions have to be taken (line 85).
Reason two - the learner comes to see what economic activity is made of and how involved it is, rather than taking it at face value (line 86).
Reason three - it supplies the tools for analysing socio-economic behaviour, meaning the behaviour of the individuals, firms and governments that the lead line has already named (line 87).
Reason four - it assists a government to push growth and development forward, which the source links with a better standard of living for the people (line 88). This is the only one of the seven that names the government itself.
Reason five - it puts the student in a position to follow and to value the different policies a government makes once choices have to be taken between them (line 89).
Reason six - its knowledge throws light on how unevenly income and opportunity are shared, and on what that inequality does (line 90).
Reason seven - it is what makes the sharing out of scarce resources between the sectors of the economy an effective exercise rather than a guess (line 91).

3. WHICH REASON SPEAKS OF WHOM
The seven reasons do not all point at the same reader, and sorting them is the quickest way to hold them in mind. Reasons one, two and five (lines 85, 86 and 89) are about the person who studies the subject. Reason four (line 88) is the one that names the government. Reasons three, six and seven (lines 87, 90 and 91) are about behaviour, sharing and allocation - that is, about the economy as a whole. The source prints its seven lines in a single unbroken list; this grouping is a study aid written for this lesson and is not the source's own arrangement.

4. THE TWO-PARAGRAPH QUESTION (line 94)
The EVALUATION that follows the topic puts one question at line 94 that asks for the reasons in two paragraphs of continuous writing rather than as a list. A model answer is given below. It is a model written for this lesson: the source prints no answer to its own question, no marking scheme and no mark allocation anywhere in Week 1, so both the answer and the marks here are proposals waiting on the teacher, and the key for the printed questions remains a separate deliverable.
Model paragraph 1: Economics is placed among the social sciences, and the source note opens its topic by saying that it studies the way people behave in the ordinary business of life - the individual, the firm and the government alike. We study it, first, for what it does to the person who studies it. It hands the student the basic skill of analysing an economic problem, and the note connects that skill with being better prepared for any post in which economic decisions have to be taken. It lets the learner see what economic activity is really made of and how involved it is, instead of accepting it at face value. And it puts the student in a position to follow and to value the different policies a government makes once a choice has to be taken between them.
Model paragraph 2: The second half of the list looks outward, to the government and to the economy as a whole. Economics is the tool that assists a government to push growth and development forward, and the note links that work with a better standard of living for the people. It supplies the means to analyse socio-economic behaviour itself, the behaviour of the individuals, firms and governments the opening line has named. Its knowledge throws light on how unevenly income and opportunity are shared and on what that unevenness does. Finally, it is what makes the sharing out of scarce resources between the sectors of the economy an effective exercise rather than a guess. Taken together, these are the reasons the note gives for studying the subject at this stage.
How the model is built, and what a marker should look for: the first paragraph opens with the lead line of 84 and then works through the reasons that speak of the student (lines 85, 86 and 89); the second takes the reason that names the government (line 88) and the three that speak of the economy as a whole (lines 87, 90 and 91). Every reason used is one of the seven the source states, nothing outside those lines is added, and the answer runs as two connected paragraphs instead of as numbered points.

5. WHAT THIS LESSON DOES NOT ANSWER
The same EVALUATION block carries a second question at line 95, asking who is regarded as the father of economics and how he defined the subject. It is not answered here. Nothing in the lines this lesson works from states either the name or the definition; Week 1 prints names and definitions in its own definitions section, and the package already holds those attributions open as unverified (ECONOMICS-T1-W01-DEFINITION-ATTRIBUTIONS), so importing a name into this lesson would teach a claim the school has not accepted. The multiple-choice WEEKEND ASSIGNMENT and the SECTION B questions of Week 1 are likewise left untouched: the source prints no key for them, and no option letter may be recorded as correct until the school authorises one.

6. HOW TO WORK WITH THIS TOPIC
Begin with the lead line, because it fixes what Economics studies and whose behaviour it studies. Then learn the seven reasons in the order the source prints them, keeping the line number attached to each. When a question asks why the subject is studied, open with the lead line, keep the reasons about the student in one paragraph and the reasons about the government and the economy in the other, and add nothing the source does not state.

lessons.title: How opportunity cost helps individuals, firms and government make choices
objectives: Explain the five ways opportunity cost supports an individual's decisions and use of scarce resources.
Explain how opportunity cost informs a firm's production method, project and policy choices.
Explain how opportunity cost informs government resource allocation, budget preparation and project execution.
Apply the next-best-alternative principle to simple individual, firm and government examples.
lessons.body:
HOW OPPORTUNITY COST HELPS PEOPLE AND ORGANISATIONS MAKE CHOICES

What you will learn
By the end of this lesson, you should be able to explain how opportunity cost helps an individual, a firm and a government make decisions; connect it with allocating scarce resources, choosing priorities and planning a budget; and apply the idea to a simple example.

How this lesson relates to the school note
The Week 3 lesson introduces opportunity cost as the next best alternative forgone when a choice is made. Week 4 lists ways this idea is useful to individuals, firms or organisations, and governments. The school note gives the lists; this supplementary lesson explains what each point means and shows how to use it. The explanations and examples below are newly written teaching material, not additional wording from the source.

1. IMPORTANCE TO AN INDIVIDUAL

An individual has limited income, time and other resources but many wants. A choice means using a resource for one purpose rather than another. Thinking about opportunity cost helps the person notice what the next best alternative will be before deciding.

• Better decision-making: compare the benefit of the option you prefer with the next best option you would give up. This makes a decision more thoughtful.
• Allocation of scarce resources: decide how to divide limited money or time among competing needs. A person cannot spend the same naira twice.
• Judicious use of resources: avoid wasting money, time or materials on a low-priority use when a more valuable alternative is available.
• Prioritising wants: rank wants so that the most important ones are considered first.
• Wise choice: make a choice with awareness of both what is selected and the best alternative sacrificed.

Worked example (hypothetical)
Ada has ₦1,000 available for one afternoon. Her two highest priorities are transport to a study group (₦600) and buying a novel (₦500). She cannot pay for both from the ₦1,000 if she also needs to keep ₦400 for food. If she chooses the study group, the novel is the next best alternative she gives up. The opportunity cost is the benefit of the novel, not automatically the ₦500 price tag. The figures are invented for this classroom example; they are not a statement about current prices.

2. IMPORTANCE TO A FIRM OR ORGANISATION

A firm also has limited resources: money, workers, machines, materials, time and workspace. Opportunity cost helps managers compare alternative uses of those resources.

• Decision-making: compare possible actions and consider the best alternative that will be forgone.
• Choosing a method of production: consider whether to use a more labour-intensive or more capital-intensive method, taking account of the resources each method uses and the alternative use of those resources.
• Project execution: select and plan projects with awareness that funds, workers and time committed to one project cannot be used for another at the same time.
• Policy formulation and implementation: when setting rules or plans, consider the alternative uses of the organisation's limited resources and the consequences of the choice.

Worked example (hypothetical)
A small bakery has a limited equipment budget. It can buy a larger oven or improve its delivery arrangement, but it cannot do both this month. The manager should compare the likely benefit of each option and identify the best alternative that will be given up. The opportunity cost of choosing the oven is the benefit of the next best option forgone. The example does not assume which option is more profitable; the manager needs evidence before deciding.

3. IMPORTANCE TO GOVERNMENT

Government must choose how to use limited public revenue, staff, land, equipment and time among many public needs. Opportunity cost helps public decision-makers make those choices openly and responsibly.

• Resource allocation: compare competing public needs and decide where limited resources can be used most effectively.
• Decision-making: identify the best alternative that will be forgone when a policy or project is selected.
• Budget preparation: recognise that money assigned to one programme is not available for another programme in the same budget.
• Project execution: plan the use of funds, workers, materials and time while considering the other projects that those resources could have supported.

Worked example (hypothetical)
A local authority has a fixed amount available for one improvement this term. It is considering repairing a community water point or renovating a public reading room. It should assess the needs, expected benefits, costs and people affected by both options. If it chooses the water point, the reading-room improvement is the alternative forgone only if it is the next best option. The example does not claim that one project is always more important; the decision depends on local evidence and priorities.

4. A SIMPLE WAY TO APPLY OPPORTUNITY COST

1. State the resource that is limited (for example, money, time, workers or equipment).
2. List the realistic alternatives that compete for that resource.
3. Decide which alternative is the preferred choice.
4. Identify the next best alternative that will not be selected.
5. Explain the benefit of that next best alternative as the opportunity cost.
6. Give a reason for the choice, such as priority, expected benefit or the needs being served.

Remember
Opportunity cost is not simply every option rejected added together. It is the value or benefit of the next best alternative forgone. It is also not automatically the cash amount paid for the chosen item. The money price and the opportunity cost answer different questions.

5. ANSWERS TO THE WEEK 4 EVALUATION

Question 1 asks for three importance of opportunity cost to an individual. Any three correctly explained points from this lesson earn credit: it improves decision-making; helps allocate scarce resources; encourages judicious use of resources; helps prioritise wants; and supports wise choice.

Question 2 asks for two importance to a firm. Any two correctly explained points earn credit: decision-making; choosing a method of production; project execution; and policy formulation and implementation.

6. ANSWERS THAT CAN BE GIVEN TO THE WEEKEND ASSIGNMENT

Item 1: option (a), “left unbought”, is the closest option given. More precisely, opportunity cost is the value or benefit of the next best alternative forgone, not every item left unbought.
Item 2: option (b), “optimum”, is the intended answer: considering opportunity cost can support better allocation of limited resources.
Item 4: option (b), “opportunity cost”, is the intended answer because it describes giving up an alternative in favour of another.
Item 5: option (c), “scale of preference”, is the intended answer because ranking wants helps a person decide which want to satisfy first.
Item 3 is not answered here. The source asks whether “nominal cost” is the same as “money cost”, but the assigned first-term source does not define either term. The school must supply or approve a reliable definition before a correct option is recorded.

7. SECTION B AND REVISION QUESTIONS

The second Section B question asks for three importance of opportunity cost to each of the economic agents. A complete answer should give three relevant points for individuals, three for firms and three for government, using the lists in Sections 1–3 above.

The first Section B question asks learners to differentiate between nominal cost and real cost. It is not answered in this lesson because those terms are not defined in the assigned source. The five REVISION/GENERAL EVALUATION questions also draw on earlier topics: ten renowned economists, the importance of a scale of preference, five reasons for studying Economics, five economists' definitions, and the difference between wants and needs. They are not silently treated as taught in Week 4. Their evidence and answer requirements remain recorded as open curriculum items.

8. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING

When you answer an opportunity-cost question, name the decision-maker, state the scarce resource, identify the alternatives, and then name the next best alternative forgone. Do not confuse the money spent with the benefit sacrificed. Use the individual, firm and government headings to organise longer answers.
